paragraphs: §1 — Recapitulation: the reward and punishment whose eternity is at issue

We recounted, in the bab before this one, the saying of its proponent regarding the reward and the punishment that come to be in the Garden (al-janna) and in Gehenna (Jahannam) — that being what attaches to the souls and the bodies together, until the world reaches the last of the time appointed for it, and the rest of the bodies pass away; then the souls come to be in the everlasting age (al-dahr) that has no expiry and no end, and they come to be in the company of the angels; and likewise the souls of the disobedient come to the spiritual punishment. And we mentioned what he adduced as proof for the perpetuity (taʾbīd) of reward and punishment, and that it is not admissible for it to be cut off, since it is a recompense from the God of the world, who has no cessation; and also his saying that the reward of God (hallowed be His names) must be complete (tāmm), and that what falls short of perpetuity is not complete — so it follows from that that the reward of God is perpetual.

: The preamble looks back to Bab 8. Taʾbīd ("perpetuation, making everlasting") is the governing technical term of the bab, paired throughout with the eschatological lexicon staged in the glossary's §VI — thawāb (reward), ʿiqāb (punishment), al-janna / Jahannam (Garden / Gehenna). Q's two opening arguments are both a fortiori from the nature of the rewarding God: (i) the recompense of an unceasing God is itself unceasing; (ii) a reward that ends is not "complete" (tāmm), and God's reward must be complete. The OCR carries a marginal numeral "1" against thawāb Allāh here, evidently a copyist's note-mark; no Hebrew citation is involved.
§2 — The "purity" argument: a terminable reward or punishment would be adulterated

And another adduced proof for that by saying that reward and punishment must each of them be pure (khāliṣ) — that is, that the reward must not be adulterated by any pain (alam) at all, and likewise the punishment must not be mingled with anything other than itself. He said: were reward and punishment terminable, then the rewarded one, whenever a portion of his reward elapsed and its cessation drew near, would grieve at that — so his reward would be impure, since it would be mingled [with grief]; and likewise the punished one, whenever a portion of his punishment elapsed and its cessation drew near, would rejoice at that — so his punishment would be impure, since it would be mingled [with joy]. But this is not the condition of reward and punishment. And since that is so, it follows necessarily that reward and punishment are neither terminable nor finite, but rather lasting, perpetual, without end and without last term.

: The "purity" (khāliṣ) argument is a phenomenological one and is symmetrical between reward and punishment: any terminus would inject its opposite affect into the experience (anticipatory grief into bliss, anticipatory relief-joy into torment), and so adulterate it. The eschatological premise that reward and punishment are by definition unmixed states is the load-bearing claim. Note that Q presents this as the argument of an unnamed proponent ("another adduced proof") — the bab is partly a doxography of the ahl al-ʿadl arguments before Q endorses them.
§3 — The "approval and wrath" argument; and the appeal to scriptural report

And another argued for that by saying that obedience (al-ṭāʿa) necessitates the approval (al-riḍāʾ) of the commander toward the obedient one, and disobedience (al-maʿṣiya) necessitates against him [the commander's] wrath (al-sakhaṭ); and approval and wrath abide so long as nothing occurs that removes each of them. And that which removes approval is the turning-back from obedience, and that which removes wrath is repentance (al-tawba) from disobedience. So if no apostasy (ridda) has occurred from the obedient one, then approval of him abides so long as the commander abides; and approval is what necessitates the reward; so as long as the approval abides, the reward abides — and that is without end, since the approving commander abides without end. And likewise the disobedient one: if no repentance has occurred from him such as would necessitate approval of him, then wrath against him abides so long as the One who is wroth abides; and since wrath is what necessitates the punishment, and wrath abides without end, the punishment is without end.

And these proofs from the standpoint of reason (min jihat al-maʿqūl) are other than what has come in the [scriptural] reports (al-akhbār) by way of mentioning the perpetuity of the two matters together, of which mention has already been made.

: The third argument grounds the perpetuity of recompense in the perpetuity of the divine dispositions of approval (riḍāʾ) and wrath (sakhaṭ): these persist unless cancelled by their respective cancellers (apostasy cancels approval; repentance cancels wrath), and where neither canceller occurs, the disposition — and so the recompense it necessitates — lasts as long as God does, i.e., forever. Al-tawba (repentance) here carries its Bahshamī technical sense (the act that lifts liability to punishment), as the glossary anticipates. Q closes the rational triad by distinguishing it from the akhbār (scriptural reports) adduced in Bab 8 — the characteristic Bahshamī-Karaite pairing of ʿaql and naql.
§4 — The Dahriyya's objection from the eternity of the world, and the kāna / yakūn reply

And the Dahriyya denied the saying of the monotheists (al-muwaḥḥida) regarding the perpetuity of reward and punishment, alleging that it contradicts their [own] saying concerning [the world's] temporal origination (al-ḥadath). That is: if it is admissible that things should be conjoined in the future, one thing after another, to no end, then it is [equally] admissible that they should have been conjoined in the past, one thing after another, to no end — so that the world would be pre-eternal and beginningless. As for one of the mutakallimūn of the monotheists — namely Abū al-Hudhayl — he embraced this objection and alleged that reward and punishment are finite and terminable. But as for the rest of the monotheists, they answered what the Dahriyya brought against them by saying: that which has a last term must necessarily have a first; and we have seen, for the things that have passed, a last term that has been reached at this present moment, so we have known by that that it [the world] has a first beyond which there is no first. But it is not [the case] that what has a beginning must therefore have an end — since its bringer-into-being and its maker is of unbounded powers; for there is nothing that He originates and brings into being but that He is able to bring into being its like without end.

So the Dahriyya said: if what has passed has all [already] been, then of what is yet to come, all of it will be — for there will remain nothing of what is-to-be that will not be; so the statement of the one who says "it [merely] will be" is annulled. And this is the strongest objection they have on this question. So it was said to them concerning that: the category of "was" (kāna) is known to have [already] occurred and been actualized; and the category of "will be" (yakūn) is likewise intelligible, [but] its annulment is not admissible — because it is an element (ʿunṣur) that perpetually goes on being existent, of which one says "it will be"; and whenever a portion of it issues forth and is actualized, there remains [still] a portion expected to be — and that perpetually, because the category of "will be" and its element are not annulled save that an annuller annul them; for were the category of "will be" to pass over into "was," the element of that whose nature is to abide and to last would be annulled.

: al-Dahriyya — the eternalists, who hold the world to be beginningless and endless (dahr = unbounded time). Their objection is a tu quoque turning on symmetry: if the monotheists allow an infinite future series (eternal reward/punishment), consistency should force them to allow an infinite past series too — which would make the world pre-eternal and so undo the monotheists' own doctrine of ḥadath (temporal origination of the world), the foundation of the cosmological argument. : Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf (d. ca. 227/841), the founder of the Basran Muʿtazila. Q reports accurately Abū al-Hudhayl's notorious doctrine that the motions of the people of the two abodes come to rest in a final, motionless repose (sukūn) — i.e., that the events of reward and punishment are finite in number (though the states then abide). Q presents him as the one Muʿtazilī who "embraced the objection" (iltazama al-muʿāraḍa) rather than answering it — conceding finitude to preserve the asymmetry of past and future. The OCR carries a marginal numeral "1" against the name. : The Dahrī rejoinder is a subtle one about the modality of the future: if everything that will be is as settled as everything that was, then the future is, in effect, already complete, and there is no genuine open-ended "will be" left to ground the claimed infinity — collapsing the asymmetry the monotheists need. Q rates it "the strongest objection they have on this question," in his characteristic habit of flagging the real force of an opponent's case. : The reply hinges on a distinction between kāna ("was" — the closed, actualized past) and yakūn ("will be" — the open, perpetually-renewing future), treated almost as ontological categories with an ʿunṣur ("element," basic stuff) of their own. The future is an inexhaustible "element": each portion that becomes actual leaves a further portion still expected, so the series never closes into "was" unless externally annulled. The OCR is rough through this passage (some clause-boundaries are uncertain), but the argument is recoverable: past and future are not symmetrical, because the past is a completed totality while the future is a non-totalizable, self-renewing potency.
§5 — Why a beginningless past is impossible but an endless future is not: the cause-and-caused argument

A portion of [what] comes to be is according to what is intelligible: namely that, whenever a portion of it has come from it and a "was"-category has issued forth, there remain of it numbers (aʿdād) [still] expected after it. This is a subtle discourse, noble in its meaning, and in it is a severance (ḥasm) of what the Dahriyya aimed at by way of equating "was" (kāna) and "will be" (yakūn). That is: what has a last term must have a first, according to the saying that preceded; but it is not [so] that what has a first must have a last, because increase (al-ziyāda) in it is possible.

And [there is] another aspect of what necessitates the distinction between what has passed and what is to come — and [the principle] that what has passed cannot be without a first, while what is going to be may be conjoined without end: namely that the last (al-akhīr) is caused (maʿlūl) — I mean that it is in need, for its coming-to-be, of the first (al-awwal); it is not found and does not come to be save by the coming-to-be of the first. As for the first, it is not caused, and has no need, for its coming-to-be and existence, of the last. That is like the one and the two: the two is caused by the one, needing for its coming-to-be the existence of the one, and not coming to be save by it; whereas the one is not caused by anything, and has no need, for its coming-to-be, of the two. And this discourse is nobler in its meaning than the discourse that preceded it; and from it may be elicited and inferred such matters as the temporal origination of the world (ḥadath al-ʿālam), the establishing of the Creator (mighty and exalted be He), and His unicity (waḥdāniyya). And we have mentioned that in the commentary on בְּרֵאשִׁית (Genesis).

: The cause-and-caused argument is the heart of the bab's metaphysics and Q rates it above the kāna/yakūn argument. A beginningless past is incoherent because each member of a temporal series is caused (maʿlūl) — it depends for its being on what precedes it, as "two" depends on "one"; but a series of caused things cannot exist without a first, uncaused member (the "one"). An endless future, by contrast, involves no such dependency in the forward direction — the "first" needs nothing later — so unbounded increase (ziyāda) toward the future is unproblematic. This breaks the Dahrī symmetry: the asymmetry of past and future is the asymmetry of cause and effect. The argument doubles as a proof for ḥadath al-ʿālam (creation in time), the Creator's existence, and His unicity — the classic Bahshamī-Karaite cosmological cluster. : The cross-reference is to Q's own Genesis commentary, the Kitāb al-Riyāḍ wa-l-Ḥadāʾiq — the same deferral-to-the-Genesis-commentary that recurs through Bab 6 (there for the free-will discussion against the Mujbira; here for the cosmological proofs). בְּרֵאשִׁית is correctly pointed in the multimodal OCR (the diff-report notes Kraken had the unpointed בראשית).
§6 — The party that denies eternal punishment on grounds of justice

As for another people: they too did not deny reward without end, but they denied that in the [case of] punishment — and that from the standpoint of justice (al-ʿadl). That is, it is not admissible, in their view, that the servant should disobey for a year, or a day, or an hour, and be punished for that for a duration that does not expire and does not pass away. They said: now if someone says, "then likewise do not [you] permit the perpetuity of reward, since it is not the right of one who obeys for a day, or a month, or a year, that he be rewarded for that for a duration that does not expire and does not cease" — we say to him: this [perpetual reward] is of the attributes of grace (al-tafaḍḍul) and beneficence (al-iḥsān), and that is of what is fitting to be ascribed to the Creator (mighty and exalted be He); whereas the other matter, which is the perpetuity of punishment, is of the attributes of cruelty (al-qaswa) and tyranny (al-jawr), and that is negated of God, the Merciful, the Just.

: The first dissenting party (unnamed; the position is close to that ascribed in the later sources to various ahl al-ʿadl and resembles the Christian/some-Jewish "limited punishment" view) accepts eternal reward but rejects eternal punishment on a justice argument: a finite sin cannot in justice earn an infinite penalty. They block the obvious tu quoque (then finite obedience cannot earn infinite reward either) by an asymmetry of divine attributes — perpetual reward befits divine grace and beneficence (tafaḍḍul wa-iḥsān, gratuitous and so not bound by strict proportionality), whereas perpetual punishment would belong to cruelty and tyranny (qaswa wa-jawr), which are negated of "the Merciful, the Just." Q will refute this in §7.
§7 — Refutation: the proofs for eternal reward equally prove eternal punishment; and the disproportion of sinning against God

And the saying of these is annulled by [the fact] that the proofs that were established for the perpetuity of reward are, in their very selves, established for the perpetuity of punishment — from reason and from report together, of what has already been mentioned. And there indicates that also [something] other than what we have mentioned: namely that we have found that whoever disobeys one whose obedience is incumbent upon him, in the manner we have explained, has thereby deserved from him some species of the punishments. And there is no [single] one of the finite punishments but that it is admissible that the one who disobeys [a master] among us should deserve it — when he disobeys a creature whose obedience is incumbent upon him — according to the measure of his disobedience. So if [the master] punishes him for his disobedience a hundred years, and he had disobeyed him a hundred years, he has not wronged him — just as, had he punished him an hour when he had disobeyed him an hour, he would not have wronged him; for these acts of disobedience may deserve the like of these punishments.

So since there is nothing among the finite punishments but that it is admissible that one who disobeys his master among us should deserve it — even though the one he disobeyed is a creature — according to the measure of the multitude of the acts of disobedience and their magnitude; and [since] we have found that one who disobeys God (glorified and exalted be He) by a single act of disobedience, were it at a single moment, [commits a thing] greater in the [estimation of] reason than the disobedience of one's master, this creature, and than the disobedience of all who disobey him among creatures throughout the length of time — [for] there is none greater in bounties upon a person than God who created him, nor more entitled to a right over him than He, and whoever's right over [a person] is greater, his disobedience to Him is greater in [the estimation of] minds — so since every finite punishment is such that it is admissible that the creatures be punished with it for what they have disobeyed, according to the measure of the magnitude of the acts of disobedience, and [since] the one who disobeyed God (mighty and exalted) has done that than which there is no [act of] disobedience greater, it must be that he deserves a punishment greater than [the finite ones], which is the lasting punishment. For everything that is terminable, we have [already] explained that one deserves it by [the kind of] disobedience [shown to] creatures; so the punishment for acts of disobedience to God (mighty and exalted) cannot but be lasting. And by the like of this it is established that His reward is lasting — that being because obedience to Him cannot but be the greatest of [acts of] obedience, since it is the worship (ʿibāda) of God (mighty and exalted), and none deserves worship save God (mighty and exalted). So since [the disobedient one] has deserved the lasting punishment — for when [God] does it, He is not wronging

: Q's own positive argument (the ahl al-ʿadl line he endorses) is a proportionality argument that turns the justice objection of §6 on its head. Two moves: (i) the §6 disputants concede that finite punishments are justly deserved in proportion to the offence; (ii) but disobedience to God is incommensurably greater than any disobedience to a creature — for God's bounty upon the person is incommensurably greater than any creature's, and the gravity of an offence tracks the magnitude of the right (ḥaqq) violated. A single sin against God therefore exceeds every finite punishment, and so deserves the only punishment greater than every finite one: the lasting (dāʾim) one. The same logic establishes eternal reward, since obedience to God is the greatest obedience — it is ʿibāda (worship), due to none but God. The section breaks off mid-clause at the foot of p249; it resumes at the top of p248 (see §7-continuation, folded into §8's opening below).
§8 — Resumption: the disobedient one wrongs himself; and the father-and-son analogy

[Resuming:] — rather the wrongdoer, the one deserving of blame, is the one who did to himself that whereby he deserved this punishment; then their punishments grow great according to the measure of their acts of disobedience, perpetually.

And of what indicates that the perpetuity of punishment is like the perpetuity of reward is that we have found disobedience to God greater in [the estimation of] reason than obedience to Him, which is its opposite — because disobedience to Him grows great on the part of the servants according to the measure of the multitude of His bounties upon them, so that it thereby becomes greater in [the estimation of] minds than their obedience. [This is] just as, if one of us had a son whom he had disciplined, taught, given possession of his wealth, and reared with the best of upbringing, and had done with him all that righteous fathers do with their children — then they saw him, after his father's bounty upon him, slack in his filial duty and his honoring [of his father] — that would not loom as great in their eyes as it would loom great in their eyes, after his father's bounty, were they to see him being undutiful to him, reviling him, and treating him with contempt. So just as the undutifulness of this son toward his father became greater in [the estimation of] reason than his filial duty, on account of the multitude of [the father's] bounties upon him, it must likewise be that the servant's disobedience to God is greater than his obedience, which is the opposite of this disobedience, on account of the magnitude of God's bounty upon him. So since the servant deserves, by his obedience to God, the lasting reward, it must be that he deserves, by the disobedience which is greater than [acts of] obedience, the lasting recompense and the lasting punishment — for it is not admissible that the recompense deserved by the small [deed] be lasting while the recompense deserved by the great [deed] be terminable.

: The father-and-son qiyās (analogy from the witnessed world, al-shāhid) reinforces §7's proportionality argument: the same ingratitude looms larger the greater the benefactor's prior kindness, so that ingratitude toward a lavishly generous father is judged graver than mere slackness. Transferred to God — the supreme benefactor — disobedience is the gravest possible offence. The OCR carries a marginal numeral "1" at bi-awlādihim. : The closing reductio: if obedience (the lesser-magnitude deed) earns lasting reward, then disobedience (the greater-magnitude deed) must earn a recompense at least as lasting — it would be incoherent for the small to earn an everlasting recompense and the great a terminable one. This seals the symmetry-of-perpetuity thesis (eternal punishment ⟺ eternal reward) against the §6 party.
§9 — The Manichaeans deny punishment altogether; the corrective-purpose objection

As for the Manichaeans (al-Manāniyya), they deny punishment altogether, and allege that a punisher who, by his punishment, neither sets aright (lā yastaṣliḥ) the one he punishes nor any other, and does not [thereby] heal his own rage (ghayẓ) — that is not admissible, because he has [then] placed the punishment somewhere other than its [proper] place. They said: because God (mighty and exalted) does not set aright the people of punishment nor any others by the punishment, and does not heal His rage by punishing them, there is no aspect of wisdom (ḥikma) in the punishment at the time of the Return (al-maʿād).

And it has been said to them concerning that: God (great be His majesty), since He is knowing that there is nothing more [effective at] restraining His servants from disobedience, nor more [effective at] calling them to the obedience to Him whereby they attain His honor, than that He threaten them, for their disobedience to Him,

: al-Manāniyya — the Manichaeans (followers of Mānī), here standing for a dualist position that rejects retributive punishment as such. Their argument is consequentialist: a punishment is just only if it serves a purpose — either correction (istiṣlāḥ) of the punished or of others, or the assuaging of the punisher's rage (shifāʾ al-ghayẓ). Eschatological punishment at the maʿād (the Return / the hereafter) can do neither — the damned are beyond reform, the saved need no example, and God has no ghayẓ to assuage — so it serves no ḥikma (wise purpose) and is therefore inadmissible. This is a recognizable form of the perennial objection to purely retributive hell. : Q's reply (which the OCR cuts off mid-sentence) shifts the locus of the punishment's wisdom from the infliction to the threat (waʿīd): the wise purpose is served not by the suffering itself but by the credible deterrent — the threat of lasting punishment is the strongest possible restraint from disobedience and incitement to obedience. The argument-form is the standard Bahshamī defense of the waʿīd (the divine threat), which requires that the threatened punishment actually be carried out lest God be charged with falsehood (see §10). The clause breaks at the foot of p247.
§10 — The threat must be truthful; and the command-and-prohibition principle

[Resuming:] — by His doing to them what they deserve thereby of the lasting punishment: then it is not admissible that He not threaten them with that and restrain them from disobedience to Him by the manifesting of this threat (al-waʿīd) — because [thereby] He will have restrained from disobedience by the utmost restraint, and called to obedience and made it desirable by the utmost incitement. So once the mention of the threat upon disobedience, by the lasting [duration] of the punishment, became obligatory — for the restraint that is in that — it became inadmissible that He threaten with the doing of what He does not do; for this is of the lying (kadhib) and the breach-of-word (khulf) that is inadmissible of God (exalted be He), and that is foul (qabīḥ) in the reason of every rational being. So it became obligatory that He do to the servants what He threatened upon their acts of disobedience, since they deserve that by their acts of disobedience to Him of the lasting punishments; and there is no blame save upon the servant who did that whereby he deserved this torment — since he was able to leave it [undone].

§10. So if they [the Manichaeans] return to answering the root (al-aṣl), which is command and prohibition (al-amr wa-l-nahy) — and that is their saying: they said that to command by what is known that the one commanded will not do it is folly (jahl); and God (mighty and majestic be He) [already] knew of the unbelievers that they would not believe; so there was no aspect of wisdom in commanding them to faith and in threatening them upon it — it was said to them: were it foul that the command [be given] to the commanded along with the knowledge that he will not obey, it would be obligatory that the command be good only along with the knowledge that the commanded will obey. But since we have found ourselves commanding one of whom we do not know that he will obey — when what we have commanded him is a [matter of] wisdom whose commanding is obligatory — we have known that it is admissible that the servant be commanded by what is known that he will not do, when the command is a [matter of] wisdom whose commanding is obligatory, in the [manner] we have explained. And the command, in the [manner] we have explained, is only not-good and foul when it is folly and corruption (jahl wa-fasād); so whenever the command is wisdom and a [thing] beneficial for the one commanded, it must be commanded — because he is able to do it, made desirous of it, made fearful of leaving it — whether it is known that he will do it or it is not known that he will do it. This is thus in the witnessed world (al-shāhid); and likewise, when the command is wisdom, and a [thing] beneficial for the one commanded, and just toward him, it is commanded even if it is known of him that he will not do it, on account of his evil choice (sūʾ ikhtiyār). And it is not admissible that two [persons] equal in limbs, in power (qudra), and in intellect, when they leave undone together two equal commands, that one of them be [a case of] justice and the other [a case of] injustice; nor that one of the two leavings-undone be tyranny and the other justice — given the equality of the two commanded [persons] and the equality of the two commands. For the knowledge that the commanded one will obey did not make the command good [merely] because He knew he would obey; rather it is good in its own self, because it is wisdom, rectitude, and justice (ḥikma wa-ṣalāḥ wa-ʿadl). And since the matter is thus in its own self, the command to one whom He knew would disobey is likewise wisdom, justice, and rectitude — even if he disobeyed through the evil of his choice, since he was commanded with the like of what the other was commanded. This is speech that has no rebuttal and no impugning.

So this [is what falls] under the head of reward and the obligation of punishment, its goodness, and its eternalization — and that [pertains] to whoever was pure in obedience, or pure in disobedience, unmixed. Let us now return to mentioning the worldly requital (al-jazāʾ al-dunyawī) and the state of one who dies while he is not pure in [his] obediences nor pure in [his] acts of disobedience.

: The §10 argument — which completes on p246 (the top of the Bab 10 file, before the al-bāb al-ʿāshir heading), so the bab is in fact complete — defends the waʿīd (threat) and the propriety of commanding the foreknowingly-disobedient: a classic qadarī/Bahshamī defense of God's commands to those He foreknows will not obey (e.g. the kuffār). The logic: (i) God's truthfulness requires that the threatened lasting punishment actually be inflicted, so the deterrent must be real, against the Manichaean attempt to void it; (ii) the goodness of a command depends on its being wisdom, rectitude, and justice (ḥikma, ṣalāḥ, ʿadl) in itself, not on foreknowledge of compliance — we ourselves rightly command those we do not know will obey; (iii) so foreknowledge of disobedience does not impugn the command, since the agent retains qudra (power) and a free, if "evil," ikhtiyār (choice), and the fault is wholly the agent's. The ʿadl axiom — that two agents equal in faculties, power, and intellect, given identical commands, cannot have one's case be justice and the other's injustice — fixes that recompense tracks the agent's own act, not God's foreknowledge. This is Q's Bahshamī free-will apparatus (cf. the anti-Mujbira material cross-referenced in Bab 6), here deployed against the Manichaean denial of punishment. The closing sentence is the explicit bridge to Bab 10 ("On retribution in this world, and the state of one who dies upholding some obediences and some acts of disobedience").

- The bab's subject and place in the sequence. Bab 9 is the first of Maqala III's eschatological babs proper. Bab 8 (preceding) argued the resurrection and the post-mortem reattachment of bodily parts; Bab 9 argues that the resulting reward and punishment are perpetual (muʾabbad) — eternal, without terminus. The glossary's §VI was staged precisely for this stretch (thawāb, ʿiqāb, istiḥqāq, iʿāda, taʾbīd, iḥbāṭ, takfīr, tawba, kabīrāt); Bab 9 supplies first attestations for taʾbīd, thawāb, ʿiqāb, istiḥqāq (the desert-vocabulary of §§7-8), tawba (§3), and al-maʿād (§9).

- Architecture. The bab has a clean three-part structure: (1) §§1-3, the constructive proofs from reason for the perpetuity of both reward and punishment (the completeness argument, the purity argument, the approval/wrath argument), capped by the appeal to akhbār; (2) §§4-5, the defense against the Dahriyya's eternity-of-the-world tu quoque, resolved by the asymmetry of kāna/yakūn and, more deeply, of cause and caused; (3) §§6-10, the refutation of the two parties who would grant eternal reward but deny eternal punishment — the ʿadl-objectors (§§6-8) and the Manichaeans (§§9-10).

- The doxographic mode. Like Bab 5/6, much of Bab 9 is doxography: Q reports the proofs as those of unnamed proponents ("another adduced," istadalla ākhar) before endorsing them, and names Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf as the one Muʿtazilī dissenter on the finitude question. This is the Bahshamī manner of giving each position its hearing; Q's own voice emerges decisively only in the refutations of §§5, 7-8, and 10.

- Q's anti-Manichaean turn. The §9-10 engagement with al-Manāniyya is notable: Q answers the consequentialist objection to retributive hell not by defending retribution-as-such but by relocating the ḥikma of punishment in the deterrent threat (waʿīd) — a move that then requires (on pain of divine mendacity) that the threat actually be executed. This is textbook Bahshamī waʿīd theology (the irreversibility of the threat against the major sinner), here imported into a Karaite eschatology.
